e-566.knowledge_point: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Velocity and Initial Position
e-566.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t) = 2t+3t^2,$ where $t\geq 0$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=1$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
e-566.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t+3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}+{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(0) = 1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =(0)^{2}+(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
x(t) = t^3+t^2+1.
$$

e-567.knowledge_point: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Acceleration, Initial Velocity and Initial Position
e-567.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t) = 1-2t,$ where $t\geq 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=1$ and velocity $v=2$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t >0.$
e-567.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1) = 2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =(1)-(1)^{2}+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t) = t-t^2 + 2.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (t-{t}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+2t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(1) = 1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}-\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}+2(1)+K \\ K & =-\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t) = \dfrac{1}{2}t^2-\dfrac{1}{3}t^3 +2t -\dfrac{7}{6}.
$$

Question 3
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with velocity v(t)=t2−t4, where t>0 is the time. If the particle is at the position x=−16 when t=2, calculate the position x of the particle at time t.

a
x(t)=112t3−18t2−16
b
x(t)=112t3−18t2
c
x(t)=112t3−18t2−536
d
x(t)=112t3−18t2−13
e
x(t)=12t−14
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives x(t)=t^3/12-t^2/8+C. At t=2, x(2)=2/3-1/2+C=1/6+C. Setting this equal to -1/6 gives C=-1/3, so option d is correct.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}-t}{4},$ where $t>0$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=-\frac{1}{6}$ when $t=2,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{{t}^{2}-t}{4})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(2)=-\frac{1}{6}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{6} & =\frac{1}{12}(2)^{3}-\frac{1}{8}(2)^{2}+C \\ -\frac{1}{6} & =\frac{1}{6}+C \\ C & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{12}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with velocity v(t)=t2−t4, where t>0 is the time. If the particle is at the position x=−16 when t=2, calculate the position x of the particle at time t.

a
x(t)=112t3−18t2−16
b
x(t)=112t3−18t2
c
x(t)=112t3−18t2−536
d
x(t)=112t3−18t2−13
e
x(t)=12t−14
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We start by integrating the velocity to get x(t):

x(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫(t2−t4)dt=112t3−18t2+C

To determine C, we use the fact that x(2)=−16. Substituting this into the above gives

−16=112(2)3−18(2)2+C−16=16+CC=−13.

Therefore, the position x of the particle at time t is x(t)=112t3−18t2−13.

content.knowledge_point: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Velocity and Initial Position
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}-t}{4},$ where $t>0$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=-\frac{1}{6}$ when $t=2,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{{t}^{2}-t}{4})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(2)=-\frac{1}{6}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{6} & =\frac{1}{12}(2)^{3}-\frac{1}{8}(2)^{2}+C \\ -\frac{1}{6} & =\frac{1}{6}+C \\ C & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{12}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Question 4

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with velocity v(t)=3t2−2, where t is the time. If the particle is at the position x=−1 when t=0, calculate the position x of the particle at time t>0.

a
x(t)=t3−2t−1
b
x(t)=t3−2t+1
c
x(t)=13t3−2t−1
d
x(t)=3t2−t−1
e
x(t)=t3−t+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start by integrating the velocity to get x(t):

x(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫(3t2−2)dt=t3−2t+C

To determine C, we use the fact that x(0)=−1. Substituting this into the above gives

−1=(0)3−2(0)+CC=−1.

Therefore, the position x of the particle at time t is

x(t)=t3−2t−1.

content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=3{t}^{2}-2,$ where $t$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=-1$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
content.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}-2)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}-2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=-1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =(0)^{3}-2(0)+C \\ C & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
x(t)={t}^{3}-2t-1.
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=6t+6{t}^{2},$ where $t>0$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=2$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t+6{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $x(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =3(0)^{2}+2(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=3{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}+2.
$$

$$

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=sin(4t)/4+C. At t=pi/8, sin(4t)=1, so C=0. Integrating again gives x(t)=-cos(4t)/16+K. Since cos(pi/2)=0 and x(pi/8)=1/16, K=1/16. Thus option d is correct.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=\frac{1}{16}$ and velocity $v=\frac{1}{4}$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{8}$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{8})=\frac{1}{4}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})+C \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(\frac{\pi }{8})=\frac{1}{16}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16} & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})+C \\ \frac{1}{16} & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{16} & =0+C \\ K & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration a(t)=cos⁡(4t), where t≥0 is the time. If the particle has position x=116 and velocity v=14 when t=π8, calculate the position x of the particle at time t>0.

a
x(t)=116(1−2cos⁡(4t))
b
x(t)=116(2+cos⁡(4t))
c
x(t)=116(1+sin⁡(4t))
d
x(t)=116(1−cos⁡(4t))
e
x(t)=116(2−sin⁡(4t))
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity v(t):

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫cos⁡(4t)dt=14sin⁡(4t)+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(π8)=14. Substituting this into the above gives

14=14sin⁡(4⋅π8)+C14=14sin⁡(π2)+C14=14+CC=0.

So the velocity is given by v(t)=14sin⁡(4t).

Now, we integrate the velocity to get x(t):

x(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫14sin⁡(4t)dt=−116cos⁡(4t)+K

To determine K, we use the fact that x(π8)=116. Substituting this into the above gives

116=−116cos⁡(4⋅π8)+C116=−116cos⁡(π2)+C116=0+CK=116.

Therefore, the position x of the particle at time t is x(t)=−116cos⁡(4t)+116=116(1−cos⁡(4t))

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option d. Differentiating gives v(t)=sin(4t)/4 and a(t)=cos(4t). At t=pi/8, these yield x=1/16 and v=1/4. The deliberately submitted option b fails both initial conditions.

content.knowledge_point: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Acceleration, Initial Velocity and Initial Position
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=\frac{1}{16}$ and velocity $v=\frac{1}{4}$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{8}$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
content.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{8})=\frac{1}{4}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})+C \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(\frac{\pi }{8})=\frac{1}{16}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16} & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})+C \\ \frac{1}{16} & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{16} & =0+C \\ K & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration a(t)=t−2t4, where t≥0 is the time. If the particle has position x=110 and velocity v=110 when t=1, calculate the position x of the particle at time t>0.

a
x(t)=13t3−112t6
b
x(t)=16t3−115t6+120t2
c
x(t)=16t3
d
x(t)=16t3−115t6+120t2
e
x(t)=16t3−115t6
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating acceleration gives v(t)=t^2/2-2t^5/5+C. Since v(1)=1/10, C=0. Integrating again gives x(t)=t^3/6-t^6/15+K. At t=1, 1/6-1/15=1/10, so K=0. Therefore option e is correct.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=t-2{t}^{4}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=\frac{1}{10}$ and velocity $v=\frac{1}{10}$ when $t=1$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (t-2{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{1}{10}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}-\frac{2}{5}(1)^{5}+C \\ \frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{2}{5}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{15}{t}^{6}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(1)=\frac{1}{10}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{6}(1)^{3}-\frac{1}{15}(1)^{6}+K \\ \frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{15}+K \\ \frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{10}+K \\ K & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{15}{t}^{6}.
$$

x(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫(12t2−25t5)dt=16t3−115t6+K

content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=t-2{t}^{4}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=\frac{1}{10}$ and velocity $v=\frac{1}{10}$ when $t=1$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
content.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (t-2{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{1}{10}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}-\frac{2}{5}(1)^{5}+C \\ \frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{2}{5}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{15}{t}^{6}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(1)=\frac{1}{10}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{6}(1)^{3}-\frac{1}{15}(1)^{6}+K \\ \frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{15}+K \\ \frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{10}+K \\ K & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{15}{t}^{6}.
$$
